query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled, post-synthesis oxidation treatment that promotes the formation of a thin, self-healing, spinel-type oxide layer on the high-entropy alloy surface will reduce both the coefficient of friction and wear rate over a wide range of service temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline high-entropy alloy (HEA) components produced by methods such as sputtering or powder metallurgy, exhibiting direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding and without a pre-formed lubricious oxide film.
generation.intervention: Perform a precise post-processing thermal oxidation treatment in a controlled oxygen partial pressure environment designed to form a thin, adherent spinel-type oxide film on the HEA surface.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under atmospheric conditions with temperatures spanning from room temperature (≈22 °C) up to at least 300 °C (and potentially higher as indicated in related work up to 900 °C) with controlled sliding loads representative of self-lubricating moving components.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, nanometer-scale spinel (or related) oxide tribofilm on the outermost surface of the alloy, which mediates friction reduction and wear protection.
generation.mechanism: The oxidation treatment induces the formation of a protective, self-healing oxide layer that minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact. This layer, owing to its spinel-like structure, offers lower shear strength and acts as a solid lubricant. Under sliding conditions, it continuously reforms or repairs minor damage, thereby reducing both the friction coefficient and wear rate across a broad temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated HEA components, the intervention is expected to lower the coefficient of friction by roughly 20–50% and decrease wear rates by at least one order of magnitude, with performance improvements observable at both room and elevated operating temperatures.
generation.baseline: Untreated HEA components that exhibit higher friction and accelerated wear due to direct metal-to-metal contact and abrasive wear mechanisms in the absence of a pre-formed lubricious protective layer.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective only if the oxide film remains stable, adherent, and self-healing under the range of operating temperatures and environmental conditions. In environments where the oxide is either overly thick, unstable due to extreme oxygen partial pressures, or chemically attacked, the benefits may not persist.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence suggests that controlled oxidation can form beneficial oxide films that improve tribological performance, precise improvement magnitudes and long-term durability under cyclic thermal/mechanical stresses remain uncertain across varying HEA compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to the controlled thermal oxidation treatment in a controlled oxygen atmosphere to form the spinel-type oxide layer, while keeping the other set untreated. Conduct tribological sliding tests under identical loads and sliding speeds across a range of temperatures (e.g., from room temperature to at least 300 °C, and if possible, higher temperatures). Evaluate friction coefficients and wear rates and compare the formation and stability of the oxide layer using surface analysis methods.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during sliding tests
Wear rate (mm³/N·m) determined from post-test wear track analysis
Surface composition and oxide layer thickness assessed by techniques such as XPS, XRD, or TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both the coefficient of friction and wear rate compared to untreated samples across the tested temperature range, or if the oxide layer degrades or fails to form as characterized, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement

Question: How does the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy change under reciprocating wear conditions at elevated temperatures, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
